Chapter 6: Communication—Building Bridges to Understanding and Intimacy
Now that you’ve laid the groundwork with self-acceptance and have a handle on the dual control model, let’s talk about the next step—open communication about your needs, boundaries, and desires.
Think of communication as the bridge that links your inner world to the intimacy you share with someone else. But let’s be honest, for a lot of us, talking about sex can feel pretty awkward—or even a little scary—especially if we’ve spent years keeping quiet or feeling ashamed.
Here’s where it all begins: effective communication starts with self-awareness. Before you even think about sharing with a partner, it helps to get clear about your own feelings, preferences, and boundaries.
Imagine it like mapping out your own landscape—figuring out what feels good, what’s uncomfortable, and what you need to feel safe and connected—before you invite someone else to explore it with you.
When you’re ready to talk, gentle honesty is your best friend. Instead of focusing on what’s “wrong,” try approaching the conversation with curiosity and a sense of discovery.
For example, rather than saying, “You never do X,” you might say, “I’ve noticed I really enjoy it when we do Y—could we try that more often?” See the difference? It’s about inviting your partner in, rather than making them feel defensive.
Here are a few simple communication tools to make things easier:
First, use “I” statements—this way, you’re expressing your own feelings and needs without blaming anyone.
Second, be specific. Let your partner know exactly what feels good or what you’d like to try.
Third, really listen. Show empathy, and be open to your partner’s perspective, even if it’s different from your own.
And finally, set aside regular, low-pressure times to talk about intimacy—pick a time outside the bedroom, so it doesn’t feel like a high-stakes moment.
Here’s a real-world example: imagine a couple with mismatched desire. Instead of letting frustration build, they schedule a weekly check-in. Each person shares one thing they enjoyed that week and one thing they’d like to try. Over time, this simple habit builds trust and eases anxiety, making it so much easier to navigate their differences.
Remember, communication isn’t just about words. Nonverbal cues—like touch, eye contact, even body language—can speak volumes. Sometimes, a gentle touch or a shared laugh says more than a whole conversation ever could.
By making communication a regular, compassionate practice, you and your partner can create a real sense of safety and mutual understanding. And when you have that, you’ll find that intimacy deepens—and your sexual experiences become so much more satisfying.
